opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the underappreciated pieces of making agents actually work in practice. When you think about what an agent is doing over the course of a long task, it's not one uniform kind of problem. It's a sequence of very different steps. Some of them are trivial: read this file, call this tool, reformat this output. And some of them are genuinely hard: figure out why this test is failing, decide on the right architecture, untangle an ambiguous requirement from the user.

If you force the model to spend the same amount of thinking on every one of those steps, you lose either way. If you set it high everywhere, the agent is slow and expensive, and honestly it can overthink simple things and talk itself into weird corners. If you set it low everywhere, it breezes through the hard parts and makes the kinds of mistakes that compound over a long trajectory. And in agentic settings, errors compound. One bad decision early on can derail the next fifty steps.

So the ideal is something closer to how a good engineer works. You don't deliberate for ten minutes about whether to run `ls`. But when you hit something tricky, you slow down, think it through, maybe consider a few alternatives before acting. Having the model calibrate that itself, step by step, gets you a much better trade-off on the latency, cost, and quality frontier than any fixed setting a developer could choose up front.

There's also a practical point. Developers building these systems often don't know in advance which parts of a task will be hard. The model is in a much better position to judge that in the moment, because it's looking at the actual state of the problem. So moving that decision into the model, rather than hard-coding it into the scaffolding, makes agents more robust and frankly easier to build. You spend less time hand-tuning and more time letting the model do what it's good at.

r001.rationale: The response describes agent tasks as a mix of trivial and genuinely hard steps, and argues the model should adjust its thinking effort to each step’s difficulty.

r002.rationale: It says errors compound across a long trajectory and that one bad decision early can derail later steps, conveying that correct decisions throughout the workflow matter to overall success.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to understand about agentic workflows is that they're not one task, they're a sequence of tasks, and the difficulty of those tasks is wildly uneven. If you think about an agent going off and doing something like fixing a bug in a codebase, there are steps in that process where the right move is basically obvious. Read this file, run this command, check whether the test passed. And then there are steps where you really need to stop and think. Why is this test failing? Is this the actual root cause, or is there something deeper going on? What's the right design for this fix given how the rest of the system works?

If you apply the same amount of reasoning to every single step, you end up with one of two failure modes. Either you're burning a huge amount of compute and latency on steps that didn't need it, and an agent that takes 30 steps becomes painfully slow and expensive, or you dial reasoning down globally and the model blows through exactly the step where it should have paused, and now you've got an agent that confidently does the wrong thing.

So the ability for the model itself to decide, in the moment, how hard to think, is sort of the thing that unlocks the whole workflow being practical. It's a bit like how a good engineer works. You don't deliberate over every keystroke. You move fast on the routine stuff and you slow down when you hit something that feels off. The models that can do that well feel qualitatively different to use as agents, because they're fast where speed matters and careful where carefulness matters, and you as the developer don't have to hand-tune that tradeoff for every step in the pipeline.

The other piece, which I think people underrate, is that a lot of the information about how hard a step is only exists at runtime. You can't know ahead of time when you're writing the system that step seven is going to be the tricky one, because step seven depends on what the agent found in steps one through six. So this really has to be a decision the model makes, not one the developer makes.

r001.rationale: The response says agentic workflows contain tasks with wildly uneven difficulty and argues the model should decide how hard to think at each step.

r002.rationale: It describes the workflow as a sequence of steps, explains that an incorrect action at a critical step can make the agent do the wrong thing, and ties overall success to choosing the right actions throughout.

astra-6.text:
When you build an agent, you’re asking a model to make a whole sequence of decisions, and those decisions don’t all need the same amount of thought. Some are straightforward—take the result of a tool call and pass it to the next step. Others involve ambiguity, planning, or deciding what to do when something goes wrong.

If you spend maximum reasoning effort on every step, the workflow can become slow and expensive. But if you optimize every step for speed, you risk making a mistake that sends the rest of the workflow in the wrong direction. So the ability to allocate effort—to recognize when to think harder and when to move quickly—is really valuable. It gives you a way to balance reliability, latency, and cost as the agent encounters different situations, instead of having to make that tradeoff once for the entire workflow.

r001.rationale: It says agent decisions vary in difficulty, with straightforward steps needing less thought and ambiguous or planning steps needing more.

r002.rationale: It describes the agent making a sequence of decisions and explains that a mistake at one step can send the rest of the workflow in the wrong direction.

sol-6.1.text:
When you’re building an agent, you’re asking the model to make a sequence of decisions, and those decisions don’t all require the same amount of thought. Some are straightforward—figuring out which tool to call or extracting something from a tool result. Others involve planning, resolving ambiguity, or deciding what to do when something fails.

If you use a fixed amount of reasoning for every step, you’re either spending too much time and compute on the easy steps or not spending enough on the hard ones. And over a long workflow, those costs add up.

So the ability to choose its reasoning effort lets the model allocate compute where it’s most useful. It can move quickly through routine steps and slow down when a decision deserves more scrutiny. The interesting question is whether it can reliably recognize those moments, because that’s what makes the trade-off work in practice.

r001.rationale: It contrasts straightforward steps with harder planning and ambiguity decisions, then says the model can allocate reasoning effort accordingly.

r002.rationale: It describes a sequence of decisions, but does not state that overall task success depends on taking the correct action at each step.
